title: Losar, the fifth time
hook: the new year: clean, renew, begin
tomorrow: a full-moon verse has three lines. why is the third about the mind?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rohatsu: a hand on the ground, an eye on a point of light at dawn. The morning star. Now the year turns over, and the old question about starting fresh.

New planners get bought, gyms fill up, and last year's resolution gets written down again, word for word. Losar, the Tibetan new year, starts with a broom instead: in the last days of the old year, houses are scrubbed top to bottom. The suttas have a clean start of their own. A monk named Samiddhi bathes in a hot spring before dawn and stands on the bank in one robe, drying off. A being appears, so bright the whole spring glows, and asks him a question: do you know the verse of the one good night? He doesn't. Learn it, the being says, and vanishes.
screen: `THE SAME RESOLUTION, AGAIN.` → `LOSAR STARTS WITH A BROOM.` → `A GLOWING STRANGER AT THE SPRING.` → `"THE VERSE OF THE ONE GOOD NIGHT?"`

segments.voice: So Samiddhi goes to the Buddha and asks. The verse, in paraphrase: don't run after the past, don't build your hopes on the future. The past is left behind; the future hasn't come. Whatever is here now, see it clearly, right where it is, unshaken. Someone who lives like that, day and night, has had one good night. Then, the sutta says, the Buddha got up and went into his dwelling without explaining a word. The monks had to ask Mahakaccana, a disciple known for opening up short sayings. His answer is the surprise. Running after the past, he says, isn't remembering. It's replaying what you once saw and heard with longing, and letting the mind be tied to it. Chasing the future is the same knot, tied to what hasn't happened. So this isn't a teaching against memory. It's a teaching against clinging, in both directions. Set beside Losar, it gives the broom a second job. In Tibetan homes, tradition says, the cleaning is a letting go: old dust and old troubles carried out the door, so the new year can start in a clean room. The point isn't to throw out the family photos; it's to carry out the clinging. A fresh year, in this teaching, isn't a year with no past. It's a year where the past stops holding the broom.
screen: `DON'T RUN AFTER THE PAST.` · `THE BUDDHA LEAVES; MAHAKACCANA EXPLAINS.` · `NOT MEMORY: CLINGING.` · `CARRY OUT THE CLINGING, KEEP THE PHOTOS.` · then, large: `A FRESH YEAR.`

segments.voice: Pick one small corner near you: a shelf, the edge of a desk, the top of a drawer. Clear it and wipe it slowly, and each time a thought of last year or next year pulls at you, bring your hand back to the surface it's on. Then sit beside the clean spot, here, now.
Losar: the Tibetan new year, begun with a broom and a clean house, the old year's troubles carried out the door.
The line for the new year: a fresh year, with the past let go, not erased. Six of seven, swept.

howItsDone: Before Losar, Tibetan families clean their houses top to bottom and carry the old year's troubles out of the house; at the new year they make offerings at the home shrine, visit monasteries and family, and share food.

notes: MN 133 paraphrased: Samiddhi bathes at the Tapoda hot springs near Rajagaha before dawn and stands in one robe drying his limbs; a deity of beautiful appearance, illuminating the whole of the hot springs, asks whether he remembers the summary and exposition of the 'one fortunate attachment' / 'one good night' (bhaddekaratta); he does not; the deity urges him to learn it and vanishes. The Buddha recites the summary and enters his dwelling; the monks ask Mahakaccana, who explains running after the past as delighting in what the eye saw and the forms then, with consciousness bound by desire and lust. Confirm the compression.
'The verse of the one good night' is one rendering of bhaddekaratta (others: 'one fortunate attachment', 'an auspicious night'). Confirm.
Losar customs voiced generally (houses scrubbed in the last days of the old year; old dust and troubles carried out the door); no dates or counts given. Confirm.
Original: ལོ་གསར (Tibetan) rather than Devanagari, since Losar is a Tibetan word. Confirm the spelling and the say-it line.
Shape: life (a fresh start this week). Mai's arc: Mai helps Ông clean the house he sold before handing it to the new owners; he cries a little in the kitchen.
Surprising fact: in the sutta, 'running after the past' means replaying it with longing, not remembering it.
